---
title: "Population 10: Non-Identical Bernoulli"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
    toc: true
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/clt_functions.R")
student_id <- 5405

# Each observation i gets its own p, evenly spaced from 0.5 to 0.9
gen_nonid <- function(n) rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = seq(0.5, 0.9, length.out = n))
# Control: every observation has the same p = 0.7 (the average p)
gen_id    <- function(n) rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.7)
```

## 1. What population am I sampling from?

Each observation is a Bernoulli (0/1) outcome, but each one has its own success probability. In a sample of size n, the probabilities are evenly spaced from p = 0.5 to p = 0.9, as the bar chart below shows for n = 20. This models situations like patients from different hospitals, where each hospital has a different recovery rate. The average p is 0.7, so the sample mean is centered at 0.7.

This population breaks the CLT’s assumption that observations are identically distributed. I chose fixed, evenly spaced p values on purpose. If I had drawn each p at random, every observation would have the same overall probability of success, and the observations would be identically distributed again.

To isolate the effect of non-identical observations, I also ran a control: identical Bernoulli observations, all with p = 0.7. The two versions have the same average success rate; the only difference is whether p varies.

```{r}
#| label: population
p_example <- seq(0.5, 0.9, length.out = 20)
barplot(p_example, names.arg = 1:20,
        main = "Success probability for each observation (n = 20)",
        xlab = "Observation number", ylab = "p")
abline(h = 0.7, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

## 2. What did I expect?

The basic version of the CLT assumes identically distributed observations, so I was unsure whether it would still work. However, the Cauchy population failed because of infinite variance, and nothing here is infinite. Every observation is just 0 or 1, and each variance p(1−p) is between 0.09 and 0.25. So I expected the CLT to still work.

Because each observation is only 0 or 1, the most discrete data possible, I expected the Q-Q staircase to be the main obstacle and the answer to be large, probably over 100. I expected the non-identical version and the control to need similar sample sizes.

## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate?

```{r}
#| label: sweep
set.seed(student_id)
results <- sweep_n(gen_nonid, n_values = c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300))
results
```

```{r}
#| label: sweep-control
set.seed(student_id)
control <- sweep_n(gen_id, n_values = c(1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300))
control
```
```{r}
#| label: sweep-confirm
set.seed(student_id)
confirm <- sweep_n(gen_nonid, n_values = seq(100, 150, by = 10), B = 50000)
confirm
```
```{r}
#| label: sweep-confirm-control
set.seed(student_id)
confirm_control <- sweep_n(gen_id, n_values = seq(100, 150, by = 10), B = 50000)
confirm_control
```

I ran both versions at n = 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, and 300 with B = 10,000. Both crossed my Q-Q threshold between n = 100 and 150, with almost identical Q-Q correlations at every n. I then tested n = 100 to 150 in steps of 10 with B = 50,000 for both versions. Both failed at n = 110 and passed from n = 120 onward.

## 4. When did it become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = 5}$$
Under my rule, the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal at n = 120 (the smallest tested value, in steps of 10). The identical control also needed n = 120.
## 5. Why did I choose that value?

```{r}
#| label: plots-compare
#| fig-height: 7
n_a <- 20    # a sample size that fails  (update after the sweep)
n_b <- 150   # your chosen sample size   (update after the sweep)

# Theory: mean = average p; SD of the mean = sqrt(average of p(1-p)) / sqrt(n)
sigma_for <- function(n) {
  p <- seq(0.5, 0.9, length.out = n)
  sqrt(mean(p * (1 - p)))
}

set.seed(student_id)
means_a <- simulate_means(gen_nonid, n = n_a)
means_b <- simulate_means(gen_nonid, n = n_b)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot_means(means_a, mu = 0.7, sigma = sigma_for(n_a), n = n_a,
           breaks = seq(min(means_a) - 0.5 / n_a, max(means_a) + 0.5 / n_a, by = 1 / n_a))
plot_means(means_b, mu = 0.7, sigma = sigma_for(n_b), n = n_b,
           breaks = seq(min(means_b) - 0.5 / n_b, max(means_b) + 0.5 / n_b, by = 1 / n_b))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

My rule requires |skewness| < 0.2, |excess kurtosis| < 0.5, and a Q-Q correlation above 0.998.

Skewness and kurtosis passed early, by about n = 20 for skewness. The Q-Q correlation was the deciding check, because the data are 0s and 1s and the sample mean can only take values in steps of 1/n. At n = 110, the Q-Q correlation was just under 0.998 for both versions. At n = 120, it was just over (0.9980 non-identical, 0.9982 control). Both displayed 0.9980 at n = 110, but the table rounds to four decimals, and the unrounded values were slightly below the threshold.

The plots show the staircase shrinking. At n = 20, the Q-Q plot has large steps of 1/20. At n = 120, the steps are fine and the points follow the line closely. The histogram also matches the normal curve well.

The main result is that the non-identical version and the identical control behaved almost exactly the same at every sample size. Breaking the “identically distributed” assumption did not slow down convergence in this case.

## 6. What surprised me?

I was surprised that breaking an assumption made no difference. I expected non-identical observations to cause problems, but the CLT worked just as well and just as fast. I learned that the identical-distribution assumption makes the basic CLT simpler to prove, but it is not strictly required. A more general version of the CLT works when observations differ, as long as no single observation dominates the total. Here, every observation has a similar, small variance, so none dominates.

This was very different from the Cauchy population, where breaking the finite-variance assumption made the CLT fail completely. So not all assumptions are equally important: infinite variance is fatal, while modest differences between observations are not.

One small difference I noticed was that the non-identical version was slightly less skewed at small sample sizes. Observations with p near 0.5 are nearly symmetric, which partly offsets the skew from observations with p near 0.9. At n = 1, the only p is 0.5, so that single observation is a perfectly symmetric coin flip.
